help.tavern.intro: The Gilded Tankard keeps three patrons with three problems on the board at any hour. Missions are the idle half of the game: they run in real time whether the tab is open, closed, or forgotten in another browser.
help.tavern.bullet.0: A job costs vigor equal to its length in minutes — 5, 10, 15 or 20. You wake with 100 vigor, a free +50 Second Wind waits behind the bar, and up to five Golden Ales add 20 each for 2 gems. A very good day is 250.
help.tavern.bullet.1: Finished rewards sit banked until you claim them, so a mission that ends while you sleep loses nothing. Each claim also rolls a 33% chance of an item and a 5% chance of a bonus chest on top.
help.tavern.bullet.2: The first re-roll of the board each day is free; every one after costs a gem. Spend the free one before you start paying for scenery.
help.tavern.bullet.3: Jobs come from your frontier zone unless you pin an older one. Pinning costs 8% of the pay per zone you step back, down to a floor of 60% — a fair price when that zone holds a pet or a codex page you still want.
help.tavern.bullet.4: Unspent vigor is gone at midnight and never banks. If the evening is ending, queue the longest job you can afford and let it run while you sleep.
help.tavern.bullet.5: Nothing else runs while a mission does — no expedition, no patrol. And patrol only opens once your vigor drops under 5, which is why "spend down, then walk the walls" is the shape of most days.
help.expeditions.intro: The active way to spend vigor: 25 of it buys five encounters of three cards each, and you decide which card gets turned over. It pays 10–15% better than missions precisely because you have to be there.
help.expeditions.bullet.0: Two expeditions a day. They cannot share the clock with a mission or a patrol, so start one when you have a quarter of an hour to give it.
help.expeditions.bullet.1: Cards come up Fight (about 60%), Treasure (25%) or Event (15%). The third encounter always offers a mini-boss as one of its three.
help.expeditions.bullet.2: Every pick adds Heroism, and Heroism alone decides the chest at the end: Bronze under 20, Silver from 20, Gold from 35. Gold chests are the only ones that can hold a set piece.
help.expeditions.bullet.3: Losing a fight never ends a run — it pays 3 Heroism instead of 8, and you carry on. The mini-boss is worth 14 against a loss of 4, which is why the bold line is usually the right one.
help.expeditions.bullet.4: Abandoning a run refunds nothing at all, vigor included. Finish it, even badly.
help.patrol.intro: The Watch only hires exhausted adventurers. Union rules: a patrol can only start once your vigor has dropped under 5, which makes it what you do with the rest of the night.
help.patrol.bullet.0: Patrol trickles gold at roughly 30% of a frontier mission's rate and experience at 10%, plus one pet treat an hour.
help.patrol.bullet.1: It pays in whole 30-minute ticks and discards the remainder, so collecting 29 minutes into a tick throws that half hour away.
help.patrol.bullet.2: Accrual stops at 8 uncollected hours. Collecting restarts the meter, which is the entire reason to check in before bed and again over coffee.
help.patrol.bullet.3: At midnight the Watch sends you home: the patrol banks itself and stops. It never spans two days.
help.patrol.bullet.4: You cannot patrol and run missions at the same time. The trickle is smaller than the vigor economy by design, so spend the vigor first and patrol with what is left of the evening.
help.arena.intro: Ten rewarded bouts a day against the realm's ladder. Every opponent is a real row in the Hall of Fame with its own level, gear and honor, and the fight resolves the instant you commit to it.
help.arena.bullet.0: Three names are offered — one below you, one at your level, one above — and they change after every bout. The odds chip on a card is a rehearsal of the fight, not a promise about it.
help.arena.bullet.1: A win puts you just above the loser's honor, but a single win can only leap so far: 15 honor, or 0.1% of yours if that is more. Walls come down through sustained winning, never one lucky upset.
help.arena.bullet.2: A loss costs a little honor and pays consolation gold. Honor never falls below 25, so one bad evening cannot undo a good month.
help.arena.bullet.3: Ten minutes sit between bouts. A gem skips the wait — a convenience, and deliberately not an edge.
help.arena.bullet.4: One win in five drops an Arena Chest at your item level, and the first time you reach ranks 500, 250, 100, 50, 25, 10, 3 and 1 the hall pays gems for it, from 5 up to 50.
help.arena.bullet.5: Once the ten rewarded bouts are spent, sparring is unlimited and free: no honor moves, no rewards, no risk. Practice stays uncapped while the economy stays capped.
help.dungeons.intro: Five wings, ten named bosses each, and no way to grind past them. A dungeon boss is a stat wall standing 15–25% above a hero on the curve — bouncing off one is the intended experience, not a mistake.
help.dungeons.bullet.0: One attempt per wing per hour. Attempts are free; the cooldown is the whole price.
help.dungeons.bullet.1: Cooldowns are per wing, so a wasted hour in the Sunken Crypt does not stop you knocking on the Rat Cellars.
help.dungeons.bullet.2: Floors 5 and 10 drop a set piece and prefer pieces you do not own yet. Every floor pays a gem when you clear it, three on the set floors, and five more for finishing the wing.
help.dungeons.bullet.3: A floor is cleared once and stays cleared. There is no farming a boss you have already beaten, which is why the wall in front of you is always the only one that matters.
help.dungeons.bullet.4: When you bounce, the answer is reliably boring: buy attribute points, upgrade a piece of gear you are keeping, come back next hour.
help.hallOfFame.intro: The realm ladder: 750 names and yours, ranked by honor. Every one of them is climbing whether or not you log in.
help.hallOfFame.bullet.0: Any row opens a person — their gear, their attributes, a fortnight of honor history. Worth a look before you pick an arena fight.
help.hallOfFame.bullet.1: The ladder lives. Names level, streak, slump, take holidays, and a couple of percent quit for good each month and are replaced at the bottom by someone brand new.
help.hallOfFame.bullet.2: Honor buys nothing whatsoever. It is a ranking and only a ranking, which is exactly what makes it safe to chase.
help.hallOfFame.bullet.3: Your row is highlighted, and the controls jump between the top of the ladder and wherever you currently stand.
help.hallOfFame.bullet.4: Catching up is a season, not an evening: the casual half goes in weeks, the top hundred in a few months, and rank 1 sits somewhere between five and eight months of serious play.
help.shops.intro: Three merchants with six things each on the shelf: the Weapon Smith and the Armorer from level 10, the Arcanum from level 12. Every shelf turns over at midnight.
help.shops.bullet.0: Shops never stock set or legendary gear — Epic is the ceiling. Sets are earned in dungeons or fished out of the well; this counter is for patching the slot that is holding you back today.
help.shops.bullet.1: One re-roll per merchant per day is free. After that it costs a gem each time, and each shop keeps its own free re-roll.
help.shops.bullet.2: The Arcanum also pours elixirs: +10%, +15% or +25% to a single attribute for 24 real hours, in three slots, never two on the same attribute.
help.shops.bullet.3: Shop gold competes directly with attribute points. Early on a weapon two rungs above yours beats the points it costs; later the sheet wins nearly every time.
help.shops.bullet.4: A full backpack blocks a purchase outright — the merchant will not hold it for you. Clear space before you go shopping.
help.forge.intro: Old Coalbeard keeps two benches: one that makes a piece of gear better, and one that turns gear into the materials for making other gear better.
help.forge.bullet.0: Upgrades run +1 to +20 and add 2.5% of the piece's base stats each, so a finished piece is half again the item it started as. Costs climb steeply in both scraps and gold.
help.forge.bullet.1: Dismantling is capped at five items a day and pays scraps by rarity — 1, 2, 4, 8, 15 — plus arcane dust from Epic and up, the rarest material in Brambleford.
help.forge.bullet.2: Upgrades do not survive the furnace. Dismantling an upgraded piece returns its ordinary scrap value and nothing for what you sank into it, so pour scraps into gear you mean to keep for weeks.
help.forge.bullet.3: Scraps are the long bottleneck of the whole game: five dismantles a day is the entire faucet, and the ladder to +20 is a bottomless drain.
help.forge.bullet.4: The five dismantles reset at midnight and do not bank. Sitting on a backpack of junk, spend them before the day turns over.
help.stable.intro: A mount shortens every mission you run, from the moment you saddle it. Wilbur rents by the fortnight, though — nothing in this stall is ever owned.
help.stable.bullet.0: Four rungs: Barley the Pack Mule at 5,000 gold for −10%, the Dappled Courser at 75,000 for −20%, the Bastion Warhorse at 1,200,000 for −30%, and the Ember Drake at 60 gems for −50%.
help.stable.bullet.1: Every rental is full price, every time. Renewing the same animal extends the fortnight; moving up a rung starts a fresh one.
help.stable.bullet.2: Mounts compress real time, never the daily cap. The same 250 vigor simply fits into fewer hours of your day.
help.stable.bullet.3: The Ember Drake is the gem decision of the early game: you start with exactly the 60 gems it asks for, so the best mount in town is a day-one choice — and keeping it saddled is the ongoing cost.
help.stable.bullet.4: Every mount hands over a small cosmetic title, and you keep the titles of the mounts you outgrow.
help.menagerie.intro: Sixteen pets, one shoulder. The equipped pet's auras are live; the ones waiting in the back room still count for something.
help.menagerie.bullet.0: Each distinct pet you own is +0.5% to all attributes, up to +8% with all sixteen. Owning is the bonus — equipping only picks which aura is running.
help.menagerie.bullet.1: Pets level from 1 to 50 on treats, and their auras grow as they do. Treats come from missions, hours of patrol, quests and the wheel.
help.menagerie.bullet.2: Switching the equipped pet is free and instant. Swap to a gold aura for a shopping evening and swap back before you fight.
help.menagerie.bullet.3: The tail is long on purpose: an aura is roughly two thirds grown by level 30, so the last twenty levels are completionism rather than a gate on your power.
help.menagerie.bullet.4: They come from everywhere — story chapters, zone mission drops at around 2%, dungeon first clears, achievements, the wheel's jackpot — and two of them live only on the well's pet banner.
help.well.intro: An old well behind the tavern. You throw gems in; it throws things back. The odds and both pity counters stay on screen at all times, and none of this has ever cost real money — there is no shop here, and there will not be one.
help.well.bullet.0: Five gems a toss, or 45 for ten — the tenth is the discount. One toss a day on the Standard Well is free.
help.well.bullet.1: Pity is kept per banner and forgets nothing: every tenth toss guarantees Epic or better, and the thirtieth guarantees a set piece.
help.well.bullet.2: The Featured banner rotates on Mondays and puts one class set on rate-up: three of every four set pieces it returns belong to that set, at the tier nearest your level plus ten.
help.well.bullet.3: The pet banner rotates every second week and carries two pets that exist nowhere else in the game.
help.well.bullet.4: Duplicates are never dead weight. Repeat set and legendary pieces become arcane dust and codex credit; a repeat pet becomes 40 treats.
help.well.bullet.5: The honest trade: spending every gem here rather than on Golden Ale costs roughly 14% of your attribute power by day 120. You are buying the collection instead — a fine thing to buy, as long as you know that is what you are buying.
help.wheel.intro: Five spins a day at the Wheel of Destiny. The first is free; the rest cost rising gold — 0.4, 0.8, 1.6 and finally 3.2 times what a ten-minute mission pays.
help.wheel.bullet.0: Twelve slots: three sizes of gold, experience, an item, scraps, treats, dust, a gem, a mystery, a 1% jackpot, and one slot that pays nothing but a salute.
help.wheel.bullet.1: The last two spins cost more gold than the wheel returns on average. That is deliberate: you buy them for the item, gem and treat slots, not to make money.
help.wheel.bullet.2: The mystery slot lands somewhere else and doubles it, but it can never land on the jackpot — and the jackpot is the only place in the realm the Gilded Snail lives.
help.wheel.bullet.3: Spins reset at midnight and never bank. A free spin you did not take is simply gone.
help.wheel.bullet.4: Every spin is a point of Activity, which makes the free one part of the daily-chest routine rather than a detour.
help.character.intro: Your sheet: five attributes, ten equipment slots, a backpack, and the only genuinely infinite gold sink in the game.
help.character.bullet.0: Attribute points are bought with gold and nothing else — levels hand out none. Each point costs more than the last, up to a ceiling of 10,000,000 gold apiece, which is how gold stays worth earning forever.
help.character.bullet.1: Your main attribute drives damage, Constitution is your health, and Luck is your critical chance (capped at 50%, or 60% for an Assassin). The other three are not dead weight: an attribute you share with an attacker blunts what they swing at you.
help.character.bullet.2: The ×10 button walks up the price ladder ten points at a time and stops the moment the next one is unaffordable, so it can never overspend you.
help.character.bullet.3: The backpack holds thirty items. When it is full, new drops are sold on the spot at vendor price rather than lost — better than nothing, and much worse than having room.
help.character.bullet.4: Elixirs sit in three potion slots for 24 real hours each and refuse to stack on the same attribute. They expire on the wall clock, not on your playtime.
help.character.bullet.5: Titles are pure prestige. They change no number at all, and they show on your row in the Hall of Fame, which is the entire point of them.
help.quests.intro: Three dailies, three weeklies and two month-long marathons, every one of them measured from things you were going to do anyway.
help.quests.bullet.0: Quests read a lifetime ledger of everything you have ever done, so progress cannot desync. Closing the tab mid-quest costs nothing, and time spent away is counted when you return.
help.quests.bullet.1: One daily can be swapped free each day, and only dailies can be swapped. Save it for the ones your class cannot do: blocking is a Warrior's trick, evading belongs to Scouts and Assassins.
help.quests.bullet.2: Dailies and ordinary play fill the Activity meter to 100, which opens the Daily Chest — gold, eight scraps and a 40% chance of a gem. This is the "did my dailies" heartbeat.
help.quests.bullet.3: Weeklies pay 3 gems each and reset on Monday. Two monthlies run at a time, marathons worth 15 to 20 gems, and two of the six in the pool hand over a set piece outright.
help.quests.bullet.4: Some counters run dry: there are only 50 dungeon floors in the whole game, so "clear a floor" eventually asks for something that no longer exists. Swap it if it is a daily; let it sit if it is not.
help.achievements.intro: Seventy feats across seven categories, most of them tiered bronze, silver and gold. This screen is not a trophy shelf — it is part of your power curve.
help.achievements.bullet.0: Every tier you claim is a permanent +3 to all five attributes, and they stack forever. Forty claimed tiers is +120 to each attribute for nothing but paying attention.
help.achievements.bullet.1: Claims are manual and never expire. "Claim all" collects everything you have earned in one press, which is the correct way to use this screen.
help.achievements.bullet.2: Final tiers also pay gems, and the signature feats hand over titles to equip on your character sheet.
help.achievements.bullet.3: Two of the sixteen pets are locked behind achievements, and nothing else in the game will ever hand them to you.
help.achievements.bullet.4: Nothing here is missable. Every counter is lifetime and keeps ticking while you ignore it, so achievements arrive on their own if you simply keep playing.
help.codex.intro: A collection log that pays rent: the monsters you have met, the item designs you have seen, and the pets, mounts and frames you own.
help.codex.bullet.0: Pages fill from where you actually go. Every claimed mission records a sighting, and expedition fights draw named monsters out of your frontier zone.
help.codex.bullet.1: Ten kills unlocks a monster's lore, which is where most of the realm's history has been hiding.
help.codex.bullet.2: Completing a zone's bestiary page is a permanent +1% gold find, and every ten item designs logged is +1% experience, up to six.
help.codex.bullet.3: An item counts the moment you see it — sold, dismantled or duplicated makes no difference. You never have to hoard a piece for the Codex's sake.
help.codex.bullet.4: Codex bonuses share the global ceilings with your gear: 40% gold find and 30% experience, counting every source together.
help.calendar.intro: A 28-day board. Log in, claim the next stamp. It is a queue rather than a streak — missing a day costs you that day and absolutely nothing else.
help.calendar.bullet.0: One stamp per day, with no catching up. Two missed evenings cannot be claimed back in one.
help.calendar.bullet.1: Days 7, 14 and 21 pay 3, 5 and 7 gems. Day 28 pays 10 gems and a portrait frame available nowhere else.
help.calendar.bullet.2: The board resets on the first of the month with a fresh theme, so a run started late will not reach day 28. The start of a month is the moment to be diligent.
help.calendar.bullet.3: Everything here turns over at your device's local midnight. Winding the clock back does not buy a second stamp — the game simply waits until real time catches up.
